blocks.text: — — — far and wide it drives off the whole crowd, and the basilisk reigns over the empty sand.

So Lucan in book 9; this is set out at greater length by Nicander, and by Archelaus in Aelian. Indeed, this animal was even placed on the heads of the gods, as μόνον ἀθάνατον [monon athanaton], alone immortal, that is, by far the longest-lived of all of its kind; and, because it kills any other animal by its breath alone, it seemed ζωῆς καὶ θανάτου κυριεύειν [zōēs kai thanatou kyrieuein], to hold the power of life and death. I note this here because the basilisk is believed to be a symbol not only of King Hezekiah but also of Christ the θεανθρώπου [theanthrōpou, God-man]. Accordingly Jonathan paraphrases the passage we are dealing with thus: Do not rejoice, all of you, Philistines, because the dominion that you served has been broken; for from the sons of the sons of Jesse the Messiah will come forth. In these words it is clear that Messiah is put for basilisk, as if the Prophet had meant Christ by the name basilisk, just as many centuries earlier Moses had signified him by the serpent raised up in the desert. In the same place Jesse stands for the word נחש nahas, which means serpent. And not without reason. For, as Kimchi observes, David's father Jesse had two names: he was called not only Jesse but also נחש Nahas. Hence in 2 Sam. XVII, 25. we read that Abigail was the daughter of Nahas, who is the same as Jesse. Therefore in Isaiah's words, From the root of נחש nahas a basilisk will come forth, the Chaldee paraphrast understood the Messiah, who was to be born from the stock of Jesse.

IV. The fourth passage is Es. LIX, 5. ביצי צפעני בקעו, They have hatched the eggs of the basilisk. Here it is taken in a bad sense, as before in a good one. For the eggs of the basilisk are crimes and wicked deeds, which, conceived in thought, are hatched through deeds. Accordingly, on this passage Kimchi says: He compares their thoughts and deeds with the eggs of the basilisk, from which, when hatched, basilisks come forth, just as their evil counsels and [col. 407] deeds are hatched. And a little later: Like the egg of a chick, which pecks at it with its beak, breaking the shell little by little [III, 193] until it comes out into the light: so they cling continually to evil thoughts until they have brought them to action. There follows in the same passage of Isaiah: Whoever eats of their eggs will die; and if one presses them, a אפעה, viper, will be hatched. Thus in the same verse the same deeds are compared to the eggs of the basilisk and of the viper. Yet it does not follow from this, as Kimchi would have it, that אפעה and צפעני are names of the same serpent. On the contrary, צפעני is the basilisk and אפעה the viper, as has been proved so far. But it is customary in Scripture for the same thing to be signified by various species of serpents. So Deut. XXXII, 33. Their wine is the gall of dragons, and the cruel poison of asps. Iob. XX, 16. He will suck the gall of asps, and the tongue of the viper will kill him. Psal. XCI, 13. You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, etc. Es. XI, 8. The infant will play over the hole of the asp, and over the den of the basilisk, etc. Es. XIV, 29. From the stock of the serpent a basilisk will come forth, and its fruit will be a flying hydrus. This should be noted against Gregory of Nazianzus, who toward the end of the Second Irenic Oration writes as if a basilisk could be produced from an addled egg of an asp. For there that most elegant writer says: Ἐπειδ᾽ ἂν τὰ ὠὰ τῶν ἀσπίδων ῥήξαντες, ἢ συντρίψαντες λόγῳ σκληρῷ, καὶ ἀντιτύπῳ, οὔρια καὶ ἀνεμιαῖα ταῦτα ἐλέγχωμεν, καὶ τὸν ἐν αὐτοῖς τῆς ἀσεβείας κρυπτόμενον βασιλίσκον εἰς μέσον ἀγάγωμεν [Epeid' an ta ōa tōn aspidōn rhēxantes, ē syntripsantes logō sklērō, kai antitypō, ouria kai anemiaia tauta elenchōmen, kai ton en autois tēs asebeias kryptomenon basiliskon eis meson agagōmen]; When, having broken the eggs of asps or crushed them by solid argument, we have shown them to be addled and wind-eggs, and have brought into the open the basilisk of impiety hidden within them. He is alluding, namely, to these words of Isaiah according to the Greek edition: Ὠὰ ἀσπίδων ἔῤῥηξαν [Ōa aspidōn errhēxan], etc. καὶ ὁ μέλλων τῶν ὠῶν αὐτῶν φαγεῖν, συντρίψας οὔριον, εὗρεν καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ βασιλίσκον [kai ho mellōn tōn ōōn autōn phagein, syntripsas ourion, heuren kai en autō basiliskon]. In these words, however, that αὐτῶν [autōn] does not refer to the asps but to those wicked men whose deeds are compared in the first hemistich to the eggs of asps, in the second to the eggs of basilisks.
